setup.intro: Every step is done twice: once in the terminal, once through IntelliJ. The terminal teaches you what git does; the IDE is where you will do it on a Tuesday afternoon.
setup.shell: Git Bash on Windows, any POSIX shell elsewhere. Commands assume you are inside the repository the step names.

tools.name: gh
tools.why: Pull requests from the terminal in stage C. Optional.

tools.name: git-filter-repo
tools.why: History rewriting in step 11. Optional until then.

tools.name: a throwaway repo
tools.why: Stages A, B and D rewrite history. Do not practise on real work.
tools.install: mkdir git-lab && cd git-lab && git init

notes.b: checkout still works and still does both jobs. This curriculum uses the newer verbs because half of “git ate my changes” is a checkout that meant the other thing.
Rewrite history freely while it is only yours. Once pushed to a branch other people build on, revert instead.

notes.h: The IDE is not a lesser git
notes.b: Blame annotations, the three-pane merge tool, the interactive rebase dialog and per-line staging are all better in IntelliJ than in a terminal. The terminal wins on scripting, bisect, and anything ending in --force-with-lease.

stages.name: Foundations

youWillLearn: The three areas: working tree, index, HEAD
Reading history: log, diff, blame, pickaxe

stages.name: The daily loop
stages.blurb: Branch, sync, undo, resolve — the four things you do every day.
youWillLearn: fetch vs pull, and pushing safely

stages.name: History and people
stages.blurb: Shaping a branch for review, and finding things in the past.
youWillLearn: A PR flow that keeps reviewers sane

stages.name: Mastery
stages.blurb: Configure git to fit you, and rewrite a repository when you must.
youWillLearn: Aliases, hooks, ignore layers, useful defaults
Purging secrets with filter-repo, and its limits
